extracted.intended_audience: academics, policy makers, regulators, and practitioners interested in federal regulation, cost–benefit analysis, and law & economics
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for how regulators and policy analysts should value human life and other consequences in rulemaking — improving cost–benefit analysis by incorporating nonquantifiable goods, behavioral evidence, ethical risk judgments, and clearer oversight procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality of cost–benefit analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Improve cost–benefit analysis, a longtime cornerstone of regulatory decision-making.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyses should be strengthened rather than treated as a mere ritual: use careful quantification where possible, acknowledge limits of monetization, and integrate additional evaluative dimensions (e.g., dignity, privacy). Sunstein argues that better cost–benefit work can make regulation both more humane and more effective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for nonquantifiable goods (dignity, privacy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Take account of variables that are hard to quantify, such as dignity and personal privacy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When benefits or harms resist monetization, explicitly identify and describe them, explain their normative weight, and include them alongside quantitative estimates (qualitative discussion, threshold/breakeven tests, and sensitivity analysis are recommended).

rubrics_metrics.name: Incorporate behavioral and psychological research
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulatory decisions about health, safety, and life can benefit from taking into account behavioral and psychological research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use empirical findings about human behavior (biases, heuristics, risk perception) to predict real-world responses to rules; avoid assuming fully rational actors. Apply behavioral insights to improve design, compliance, and expected impacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for people’s fallibility
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design regulations that anticipate and mitigate human error and limits (e.g., defaults, nudges, redundancy), rather than relying on idealized decision-makers. Describe how rule design addresses predictable mistakes and cognitive limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on human consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: An insistent focus on the consequences of our choices; the ‘real world’ of cost–benefit analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Center analyses on concrete effects on life, health, dignity, and welfare. Emphasize outcomes experienced by people rather than abstract or purely fiscal metrics, and make the linkage between regulatory choices and human impacts explicit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use breakeven analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize the role of break-even analyses in government regulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply breakeven tests to determine the magnitude of unquantified benefits required to justify a regulation given estimated costs (Appendix D contains examples). Useful for dealing with uncertain or hard-to-quantify benefits: show thresholds and sensitivity ranges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Valuing mortality and morbidity (values for mortality and morbidity / VSL)
rubrics_metrics.description: Include values for mortality and morbidity when estimating regulatory benefits (Appendix E: Values for Mortality and Morbidity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use accepted approaches (e.g., value of a statistical life, quality-adjusted life years) with transparent sources and ranges; present alternative valuations and sensitivity analyses so policy conclusions are robust to plausible VSL/morbidity values.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider the morality of risk
rubrics_metrics.description: Attend to ethical considerations in distributing and accepting risks ('The Morality of Risk').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beyond aggregate cost–benefit sums, analyze who bears risks, fairness across populations, and whether certain risks are morally unacceptable. Make ethical trade-offs explicit and incorporate them into decision rationales.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for risk perception and emotion ('what scares us')
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain and incorporate findings about what scares people and what does not, since perception affects policy relevance and compliance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that public fear and perceived dread can affect acceptability and behavior; regulators should measure and, where appropriate, adjust for mismatches between statistical risk and perceived risk when designing communication and interventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency and procedural clarity in oversight (how OIRA works)
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe and make clear the procedures and analytics by which oversight bodies (like OIRA) approve regulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document decision processes, analytic methods, and institutional checkpoints; reference governing instruments (e.g., Executive Order 13563) and provide accessible explanations of how trade-offs were weighed to increase legitimacy and accountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance pragmatic resource constraints with respect and dignity
rubrics_metrics.description: Balance pragmatic concerns of resource scarcity with principled ideals of respect and dignity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policies should explicitly weigh efficiency/resource limits against commitments to respect human dignity; present how trade-offs are made and seek solutions that protect dignity within fiscal/administrative constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ground regulation in empirical, real-world examples and data
rubrics_metrics.description: Use real-world examples and current events to illustrate and test regulatory reasoning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Support analytic claims with empirical cases, data, and illustrative examples (as Sunstein does throughout the book) to show how principles apply in practice and to reveal practical complications and side effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include environmental valuations such as the Social Cost of Carbon
rubrics_metrics.description: Incorporate estimates like the Social Cost of Carbon in environmental regulatory valuation (Appendix B: The Social Cost of Carbon).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use best-available SCC estimates, explain their derivation and uncertainties, and show sensitivity of regulatory conclusions to different SCC values; integrate environmental externalities into benefit–cost frameworks.
